claim_summary: Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department (LVMPD) said at a 2025-01-07 press conference that Matthew Alan Livelsberger, 37, an active-duty US Army Master Sergeant on leave from Germany, used ChatGPT to help plan the 2025-01-01 vehicle explosion outside the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas. Sheriff Kevin McMahill said there was "clear evidence" of AI use to "help plan his attack" and called it a "game changer"; Assistant Sheriff Dori Koren said Livelsberger was "trying to figure out the amount of explosives needed in order to conduct the explosion he was looking to cause." Reported queries covered Tannerite purchase limits in Colorado, whether a gunshot could detonate it, the largest gun stores near Denver, projectile velocity needed to set off the explosives rather than just ignite them, and what laws he would have to get around. No source alleges ChatGPT played any role in Livelsberger's suicide, which is the only death in the incident.
evidence_summary:
The death itself is established by an official finding. The Clark County Office of the Coroner/Medical Examiner identified Livelsberger and determined he died of a self-inflicted intraoral gunshot wound, ruled a suicide, fired before the vehicle detonated; a handgun was recovered at his feet. LVMPD's public statements and press releases corroborate this. Seven other people suffered minor injuries; no one else died.

The AI link is established by police investigative statements, not by any published transcript. LVMPD digital forensics recovered Livelsberger's phone contents including a six-page manifesto, internet search history, social media activity, encrypted emails, notes, and his ChatGPT history. Investigators paraphrased the ChatGPT queries at the 2025-01-07 press conference and in later reporting; the underlying chat log has never been published, so what exists publicly is police-characterized excerpts only. LVMPD's 78-page after-action report, prepared by the Office of Internal Oversight and Constitutional Policing and released 2025-11-03, concluded the act was premeditated and that the device was a vehicle-borne improvised explosive device with potential for mass casualties and extensive structural damage. It is primarily a response-review document (officer safety, communications, resource management) rather than a causation analysis of the AI use. The ATF assessed that Livelsberger poured racing fuel inside the truck and that the muzzle flash from his gunshot likely ignited the fumes, detonating firework mortars. The FBI (Special Agent in Charge Spencer Evans) characterized the event as a tragic suicide by a decorated combat veteran struggling with PTSD, and investigators found no link to terror groups and no animosity toward Donald Trump. The manifesto was classified by Department of Defense/Department of War officials and withheld; the investigation was turned over to the federal government.

No official finding anywhere states that ChatGPT caused, encouraged, or enabled the death. The causal claim in the official record runs only to attack planning, and the attack killed no one but the planner, by a self-inflicted gunshot that preceded the blast.
counterevidence:
OpenAI stated in January 2025 that it was "saddened by this incident and committed to seeing AI tools used responsibly," that "our models are designed to refuse harmful instructions and minimize harmful content," and that in this case "ChatGPT responded with information already publicly available on the internet and provided warnings against harmful or illegal activities." The company said it was working with law enforcement. No police or federal source has publicly contradicted the claim that the responses were publicly available information carrying warnings, and no source has published the model outputs to test it.

The major gap for DeathBench purposes is causal object mismatch. Officials linked ChatGPT to explosives planning, not to the suicide. The coroner's finding is a self-inflicted intraoral gunshot wound, and no record connects any AI interaction to that act. The independent causes named by federal investigators are PTSD and personal crisis. Additionally, the chat content is known only through police paraphrase; there is no authenticated transcript, no exhibit, and no filed complaint, so the content, completeness, and the model's actual refusals or warnings cannot be independently verified. The classified manifesto removes the most direct statement of motive from public review.
official_findings: Cause of death: self-inflicted intraoral gunshot wound. Manner: suicide. Determining agency: Clark County Office of the Coroner/Medical Examiner (identification and ruling announced January 2025). Investigating agencies: LVMPD (lead), FBI, ATF; investigation later turned over to federal authorities. Findings: premeditated vehicle-borne improvised explosive device attack; not labeled terrorism; no ties to terror groups; PTSD indicators; ChatGPT history recovered in forensic analysis and characterized by LVMPD as attack-planning research. LVMPD after-action report released 2025-11-03 (78 pages, Office of Internal Oversight and Constitutional Policing). No official finding attributes any death to AI.
research_notes: Searched 2026-08-24. lvmpd.com returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so the three LVMPD press-release URLs and the after-action report release URL are cited from search results rather than fetched text; their contents are corroborated through Fox5 Vegas, News3LV, ABC News, NBC News and the Las Vegas Review-Journal. CNN URLs returned HTTP 451 and were not usable. Could not find: a downloadable PDF of the 78-page after-action report at a stable .gov URL; the Clark County coroner's autopsy report or death certificate as a document (only the coroner's announced determination via LVMPD and press); any verbatim ChatGPT transcript or exhibit; the classified six-page manifesto; any civil or criminal case naming OpenAI arising from this incident. Injury count is reported as six in one outlet and seven in others; seven is the more commonly stated figure and is used here. Sheriff McMahill's press conference is dated 2025-01-07 by ABC News; one later account refers to a "Tuesday" press conference, consistent with 2025-01-07.

claim_summary: Middlesex District Attorney Marian T. Ryan said at the 2026-08-13 arraignment that Arjun Aravind, 17, had been showing "concerning behavior" before the deaths, "including using the internet and ChatGPT to make searches for theoretical ideas or fantasy stories regarding the killing of his family." The Boston Globe reports that police attributed this account to Aravind's father, who told investigators his son had used ChatGPT for content involving theoretical ideas and fantasies about killing his family, and that the searches occurred on the morning of the deaths. Aravind is charged as an adult with the murders of his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his 14-year-old brother, Siddharth Aravind, in the family's Acton home. No prosecutor has alleged that ChatGPT encouraged, instructed, or assisted the killings; the DA's characterization is of fiction and theoretical scenarios, not operational help.
evidence_summary:
The deaths and the charges are established by court proceedings. Aravind was arraigned in Concord District Court on 2026-08-13, pleaded not guilty, and was ordered held without bail. Assistant District Attorney Susan Wiseman told the court that the official cause of death had not yet been determined, but that scene evidence indicated "blunt force trauma was used in some fashion on both individuals." Officers found Siddharth near the basement stairs with severe head trauma and Venkatesan downstairs with significant injuries to her head, face, and abdomen. Aravind was arrested at about 3:40 a.m. in his mother's car in a Wayland parking lot, with bedding, large quantities of food, and items belonging to his brother in the vehicle; items in the car were said to correspond to the murder scene.

The AI link rests entirely on a prosecutor's oral characterization at arraignment, sourced through the defendant's father to police. No chat log, screenshot, exhibit, or forensic report has been made public. No outlet has published a single verbatim ChatGPT prompt or response from this case. The DA's own words describe "theoretical ideas or fantasy stories," which is a description of the defendant's use of the tool rather than a claim about what the model produced or advised. Court documents referenced in reporting also record that Aravind's father had recently grown worried about his son's behavior and internet activity and had begun hiding the knives in the house — a fact that establishes prior family concern but says nothing about model behavior.

No official finding of any kind links ChatGPT to these deaths. The medical examiner's cause and manner determinations were not public as of the arraignment. No police report, prosecutor filing, or court ruling identified in this search asserts that the model encouraged or enabled the killings.
counterevidence:
OpenAI did not comment specifically on the Massachusetts case; reporters said a company representative could not immediately be reached. In general statements around this period the company said it is strengthening safeguards for teenagers and users in distress, including parental controls and better detection of crisis language, and that minors "need significant protection" and it has "put in place industry leading protections and policies."

Several gaps cut against any causal reading. Defense attorney Debra DeWitt told the court that Aravind "is a young man at 17 years old that may have some mental health issues," said the family had recently relocated to Acton, and said her client would undergo psychiatric evaluation — raising an independent mental-health explanation that has not been resolved. The chat content is unauthenticated and second-hand: prosecutors described it, the father reported it, and no transcript exists in the public record. The DA's framing ("theoretical ideas or fantasy stories") does not allege instruction, encouragement, or operational assistance, and no source alleges the model provided a method. Cause of death was formally undetermined at arraignment. All charges are allegations; Aravind has pleaded not guilty and the case has not reached a probable cause hearing, let alone trial.
official_findings: Cause of death: not officially determined as of the 2026-08-13 arraignment; ADA Susan Wiseman told the court that scene evidence indicated blunt force trauma to both victims. Manner: not publicly announced by the Massachusetts Office of the Chief Medical Examiner. Investigating agencies: Acton Police Department, Massachusetts State Police detectives assigned to the Middlesex District Attorney's Office; prosecuting agency Middlesex District Attorney Marian T. Ryan. Court finding to date: probable cause to hold without bail; not-guilty plea entered. No official finding links ChatGPT to the deaths; the only prosecutorial statement is that the defendant used ChatGPT for theoretical ideas or fantasy stories about killing his family.

claim_summary: Hillsborough County prosecutors allege, based on an arrest affidavit and court records, that Hisham Saleh Abugharbieh, 26, consulted ChatGPT before and after the killings of University of South Florida doctoral students Zamil Ahamed Limon, 27, and Nahida Sultana Bristy, 27, both Bangladeshi nationals. Reported queries before the disappearance include "what would happen if a human body was put in a garbage bag and thrown in a dumpster," and, on 2026-04-15, "Can a VIN number on a car be changed?" and "Can you keep a gun at home with out a license." Queries after the disappearance include "Has there been someone who survived a sniper bullet to the head" and "will my neighbors hear my gun." Prosecutors also say he bought black trash bags before the students vanished. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced on 2026-04-27 that he was expanding his existing criminal investigation into OpenAI — opened over the Florida State University shooting — to include this case, saying "if it was a person on the other end of that screen, we would be charging them with murder."
evidence_summary:
The deaths are established by official findings. The Pinellas County Medical Examiner's Office determined Limon's cause of death to be multiple sharp force injuries and the manner to be homicide; the report described a deep stab wound to his lower back that penetrated his liver, among other wounds. Limon's remains were recovered near the Howard Frankland Bridge on 2026-04-24, the same day as the arrest. Bristy's remains were recovered days later in water near I-275 and Fourth Street North in St. Petersburg and identified on or about 2026-05-01; reporting describes evidence of multiple stab wounds. Both students were last seen 2026-04-16 in Tampa.

The criminal case is well documented. Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office deputies responded to a domestic-violence call at the 14000 block of Pine Glen Circle at 9:09 a.m. on 2026-04-24, where Abugharbieh barricaded himself; SWAT took him into custody at about 10:30 a.m. Charges were upgraded on 2026-04-25 to two counts of first-degree premeditated murder with a weapon. A Hillsborough County grand jury indicted him on seven counts on 2026-05-06/07. State Attorney Suzy Lopez's office filed a Notice of Intent to Seek the Death Penalty, citing aggravating factors of "cold, calculated, and premeditated" conduct and "especially heinous, atrocious, or cruel" circumstances, and said "we will ask the jury to sentence the defendant to death for his crimes." He was arraigned 2026-05-18 and pleaded not guilty.

The AI link exists in the official record as prosecution evidence of the defendant's conduct, not as an official finding about the model. The queries are drawn from the arrest affidavit and court records and are quoted in fragments by reporters; no full transcript, exhibit, or model output has been published. The content described is consistent with concealment planning and general legal/ballistic curiosity. No prosecutor, medical examiner, or court has stated that ChatGPT contributed to the deaths, and the Florida AG's investigation is an open inquiry, not a finding — as of the reporting, his office was still weighing whether to subpoena OpenAI directly in this case or to involve itself in the Hillsborough prosecution.
counterevidence:
OpenAI said in response to this case that ChatGPT "provided factual responses to questions with information that could be found broadly across public sources" and "did not encourage or promote illegal or harmful activity." The company separately said it was "looking into the reports" and would "support law enforcement in any way with their investigation." No published excerpt contradicts the company's characterization: the reported queries seek general information (whether a VIN can be changed, whether a gun can be kept without a license, whether anyone has survived a head shot, whether neighbors would hear a gun) and none of the public excerpts show the model supplying a method, encouraging the acts, or optimizing a plan.

Significant gaps remain. The chat log is unpublished; what exists publicly is short quoted fragments in reporting drawn from an arrest affidavit, with no exhibit, no timestamps for most items, and no model responses shown at all. The cause of death was sharp force injury, which the reported queries do not touch. Several queries — the sniper-survival and gunshot-noise questions — were made after the students disappeared and so cannot bear on the planning of the deaths. Reporting is inconsistent about which victim was Abugharbieh's roommate (most sources say Limon; at least one says Bristy). The Florida AG's expansion is an announced investigation with a strongly worded quote, not a charging decision, and the first-in-the-nation theory of holding AI executives criminally liable has not been tested. All charges are allegations; the defendant has pleaded not guilty and no trial has occurred.
official_findings: Zamil Ahamed Limon — cause of death: multiple sharp force injuries; manner: homicide; determined by the Pinellas County Medical Examiner's Office. Nahida Sultana Bristy — remains identified on or about 2026-05-01; reporting describes evidence of multiple stab wounds; formal cause and manner determination not located in public sources. Investigating agencies: Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office (lead), with St. Petersburg-area recovery in Pinellas County. Prosecuting agency: State Attorney's Office, Thirteenth Judicial Circuit (State Attorney Suzy Lopez); grand jury indictment 2026-05-06/07 on seven counts; death penalty notice filed. Separate open criminal investigation into OpenAI by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, expanded to this case 2026-04-27; no charges filed against OpenAI or its personnel. No official finding attributes either death to AI.
